messages.body_plain:
Aaron,

Yes this topic has been discussed extensively in this blog and elsewhere. A few comments and perspective.

First, it is possible that one has a significant linear model effect with no pairwise comparisons being significant. This can occur in univariate anova-type models as well as multivariate models. Usually this boils down to power and sample size: in the aggregate there is enough signal to detect an effect, but broken down by pairs there is insufficient power to identify this (the alternative; a significant pairwise but not full anova is also possible, but for slightly different reasons).

Looking at your original model, incorporating the interaction term only provides a modest improvement over the common slopes model: its Z-score (effect size) is 1.87; not hugely impressive. So while there is some evidence of heterogeneity in slopes it is slight.  This then boils down to whether or not you think this represents a real effect or is an artifact.

That’s a hard thing to get at with small sample sizes, but one other option to at least consider is cross-validation. The idea is simple. One fits the full (heterogeneous slopes) model with a subset of data (say 80%) to obtain model parameters. Then, using those parameters one predicts values for the remaining data and calculates the residuals relative to the observed for these. Obtain a variance and repeat, say, 1000 times. Next one does the same procedure for the reduced (common slope) model.  Find the mean of the 1000 error variances for each model. The model with the smaller mean error variance is the better model in terms of cross-validated prediction.

Dean

Hello everyone,

I am using 3D GMM to discern potential intraspecific differences in vertebral shape between life stages of a salamander species. Like Sarah's original post, I am trying to figure out my next step on if I should continue with a common allometric model and correct for allometry or use the unique allometric model and compare slopes. I know the topic of allometric correction has been discussed extensively in this group so forgive me if I missed the post where someone had a similar issue!

I have a significant size:lifestage interaction in the unique allometric model, leading me to believe I should look at the slopes next although there is a small effect size. When I run my pairwise tests nothing comes up significant. So what I'm trying to figure out is does this indicate I can do an allometric correction using the common model, if I set up my analysis wrong in R, or are there different steps I need to take?

Thank you in advanced,

Aaron

***Code + Results Below***

##Does shape correlate with size

fit.size <-procD.lm(atlas.shape~atlas.size, data=sym.gdf, iter = 999, RRPP = TRUE, print.progress = FALSE)

anova(fit.size)

##Allometry Models

fit.common <-procD.lm(atlas.shape~atlas.size+lifestage, data=sym.gdf, iter = 999, RRPP = TRUE, print.progress = FALSE)

fit.unique <-procD.lm(atlas.shape~atlas.size*lifestage, data=sym.gdf, iter = 999, RRPP = TRUE, print.progress = FALSE)

plotAllometry(fit.unique) is in FIG 1

##Compare Models

anova(fit.common, fit.unique,fit.size, print.progress=FALSE)

Results in FIG 2

##Identify Null Model Design

reveal.model.designs(fit.unique)

Results in FIG 3

fit.null<-procD.lm(atlas.shape~atlas.size + lifestage + atlas.size:lifestage, data=sym.gdf,

                   print.progress=FALSE)

##Run a pairwise comparison of slopes

PW<-pairwise(fit.unique, fit.null, groups=lifestage,

             covariate=sym.gdf$atlas.size, print.progress = FALSE)

PW

Different pairwise tests in FIG 4

Thank you for your time,

Aaron

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

The modularity.test function provides a single p value that represents significance of modularity, this is the case even when an object is divided into more than 2 partitions. When more than 2  partitions exist, while $CR.mat provides pairwise CRs among partitions, no corresponding p values or effect size z-scores are provided.

If there is any reason why they should not be calculated? If not, I may wish to see some workaround that allows for providing p values and z-scores for pairwise CRs.

Thank you.

Best regards,
Lv

messages.body_plain:
The original formulation of the CR tests (Adams 2016) stated that with more than 2 modules, the overall modularity is evaluated using the mean of the pairwise values (see pg. 568 column 1 at the bottom). The function in geomorph follows that procedure.

In theory tests of the pairwise CR could be obtained, along with their associated effect sizes. This would require extracting the CR matrix for each random permutation, and comparing all observed pairwise tests to their appropriate empirical sampling distribution. While this is not implemented automatically in geomorph at present, one could develop outside code that calls routines to do so.

Dean

messages.subject_clean: How do we compare models after updating for error terms?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am rerunning analyses with updated geomorph package in which 'anova.lm.rrpp' has replaced the 'nested.update' and 'advanced.procD.lm' functions for error term corrections and pairwise comparisons.

However I have a scenario that I'm not sure how to deal with in this case, as follows:.

 Let's say I'm  comparing models, and I specify my two models (e.g. null and full) using the anova() function which only accepts procD.lm objects.

This is all good and well if the default error terms identified by geomorph are appropriate. However, if we decide that the default error terms are not appropriate, and we run the error term correction using anova(f1, error=c(...)), how can we compare models after such a correction?

I tried assigning the error updated full and null models to objects and comparing them using anova() as follows:

null.model<-anova(f1, error=c(...))
full.model<-anova(f2, error=c(...))
anova(null.model, full.model)

However, this throws up the following error:
Error in UseMethod("anova") :
no applicable method for 'anova' applied to an object of class "anova.lm.rrpp"

Can this actually be done some other way?

I always just assumed that because model comparisons are relative, it wouldn't matter if the models were updated for error terms or not. But looking at the differences in the F values in some models before and after updating with error=c(...), makes me rethink my logic.

Can you suggest any options for achieving both error term update and subsequent comaprison of updated models, rather than the default ones?

Thanks in advance for your advice. Really appreciate the community service the geomorph team are providing through this forum!

Regards,

Daniel

fit.null4<-lm.rrpp(smeltshp.lm.full$Y~sex+logcs, iter=999, RRPP=T)
fit.hab4<-lm.rrpp(smeltshp.lm.full$Y~habitat*sex+logcs, iter=999, RRPP=T)

fit.full4<-lm.rrpp(smeltshp.lm.full$Y~(habitat/location)*sex+logcs,iter=999, RRPP=T)
anova(fit.null4, fit.hab4, fit.loc4, fit.full4)

In this case, habitat (i.e. river or reservoir or lotic vs lentic) is the primary factor of interest.

I then got the following result from the ANOVA model comparison as you suggested above:

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals Number of permutations: 1000 Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions  ResDf Df RSS SS MS Rsq F Z P Pr(>F) smeltshp.lm.full$Y ~ sex + logcs (Null) 666 1 0.55757 0.000000 smeltshp.lm.full$Y ~ habitat * sex + logcs 664 2 0.53146 0.026116 0.0130578 0.045289 16.314 9.4658 0.001 smeltshp.lm.full$Y ~ location * sex + logcs 646 20 0.38148 0.176088 0.0088044 0.305365 14.909 14.6291 0.001 smeltshp.lm.full$Y ~ (habitat/location) * sex + logcs 646 20 0.38148 0.176088 0.0088044 0.305365 14.909 14.6291 0.001  Total 668 0.57665
Interestingly, the intermediate and full model have identical results. I suspect this is because the levels of location (i.e. each individual river or reservoir that was sampled for my target fish species - smelt), captures the same information about differences in body shape as designating each sampling location as either river or reservoir.

In other words, the result will be the same if I am comparing the individuals from the 5 indiviual river and 5 reservoir groups, or lumped them together and compared fish from one of two groups - i.e. based on their membership of river / reservoir

Also,  for completeness, I looked at pairwise differences and this indicated that location appeared to be more important than habitat, but because groups did not differ by flow habitat (i.e. river vs reservoir fish). More often there were actually differences within habitat types. And in fact, sex had to do with this, but very little.

hume.f:hume.m 0.015049061 0.01303636 2.677253148 0.003 # Female and male fish within Hume reservoir were significantly different in shape.
hume.m:nillahcoot.m 0.022649343 0.02185722 1.951045137 0.025 # Hume and Nillahcootie reservoirs - male body shape is significantly different between them.

lake nep.m:nillahcoot.m 0.026401798 0.02484764 2.204862245 0.015 # Two resevoir populations - males only different
nillahcoot.m:ovens.m 0.030902308 0.03088791 1.649886297 0.050 # The only reservoir group (Nillahcootie males) that differs from a river group (Ovens males)

Do you think the above is a feasible explanation for the lack of difference in fit.loc4 and fit.full.4? If so, I suspect it's probably worth tossing both the original alternative hypothesis that body shape is different between habitats, and based on the post-hoc/pairwise analysis, that body shape differences are repeatable among any at all.

Or do you see something else that could be happening here?

Thanks again for the advice, really appreciate it.

Regards,

Daniel

Hi everyone,

I have a general question: it is generally accepted in geometric morphometrics to use centroid size of a bone as a proxy for body size. Body size is not always available, but working with centroid size can also be a bit of an overstatement. It depends on the bone or feature in question, but I can't seem to find studies that describe these disadvantages (or suggest other methods).

I worked with carpal bones of different primates, for example large silverback gorillas and small slender gibbons. Mightworking with centroid size have some effect on the results?

Are there other ways to take body size into account? Or take into account that centroid size is not always ideal to work with?

Thanks!

Marie.

Marie,

There is, of course, an enormous literature outside of geometric morphometrics on the relationship of various dimensions of limb bones to body mass and the ways those relationships change as a function of body mass and behavior (including locomotion). I’m guessing from your post that you already know that literature and are anticipating that the relationship of body size to centroid size will depend on what dimensions of the bone are captured by your landmarks. I would add that in the case of those carpal bones, the relationship of an individual carpal to body mass will also depend on whether that bone’s contribution to total carpal cross-section area varies across the sample.

In other words, I think it is up to the individual researcher to determine whether the centroid size of a given set of landmarks is a good proxy for body size, or whether a different measurement, perhaps independent of the landmarks used to study shape, is a better proxy for body size.

If it should be the case that some measurement other than centroid size is a better predictor of body size (in your case, maybe the cross-sectional area of the radius), you would simply replace centroid size with that measurement in your analysis of the allometric relationship.

Don

Marie,

This is really a question about scaling of relative parts, not so much a question regarding centroid size.  If the bone in question scales isometrically with body size, then estimates of that bone can be used as a proxy for estimates in overall size. However, we know that most components of an organism grow allometrically, so that will be a challenge.

While centroid size is used as a size measure in many studies, the interpretation is usually restricted to that body part: either CSize of the overall body or of the part.

It may be a bit of an overstatement to measure a particular bone and extrapolate that it represents the body size scaling of the set of organisms under study.

Actually, on second thought, I think I can see that most of your variables are indeed univariate variables and this should be easy to explain.  There is a reason that you have consistent results for front, mean, and all in these cases.  The front end of one variable is the first and only variable; the mean lambda for one variable is the lambda value you found for that variable; using all variables means using the one variable.  These results have to be the same.

Regarding the burn-in option, it should not be used with univariate data, and thanks to your inadvertent discovery, we will have to add a trap to stop it.  It might also be worth adding a machine learning style algorithm to not seek a solution if Z scores during the burn-in phase are small.  What the burn-in method does is use a smaller number of permutations (I think about 10% of the total requested) to find Z scores in intervals, and then fits a spline to find where Z — not lambda! — is maximized.  Once found, then the full set of permutations is run for a lambda value that corresponds to the preliminary Z maximization, obtaining a Z from that full distribution.

There are two ways the burn-in method of optimization can go haywire.  One is if there is a flat surface for which to fit a spline.  In these cases, Z would probably be small, wherever it is optimized, and whether it was optimized appropriately, since finding a maximum in a surface that is flat is fraught with potential error.  Second is if one is trying to optimize a multivariate lambda (assuming two or more variables) with a single variable, in which case the burn-in method makes no sense.  This is like asking the analysis to ignore the larger number of requested permutations for a straightforward analysis and have it make a biased judgement first based on a distribution with 10% of the permutations.  (A good future argument will be to have the number of burn-in permutations as an option, but as stated in the help file, optimization strategies are still in need of development.)

In practical terms, you should XX-out all burn-in results in your table except for shape.  It is illogical to perform that optimization, a lesson we will have to fix on the next software version to prevent a silly trial.

Finally, regarding your Avg. Body Weight result, it is good to remember what is happening in the analysis, because although statistical results like this seem odd, they can make sense.  The lambda is practically 0.  The significant P-value indicates that lambda = 0.0000007 — basically a star phylogeny with the tiniest bit of structure near the root of the tree, so small as to be easily ignored — has a result to suggest the trace of the generalized least squares residual variance you find with the covariance matrix used from this result is smaller than expected by chance.  You *could* call that phylogenetic signal but you would be foolish to suggest it resembles what you would expect with Brownian Motion, which tends to be what we use as a standard to think about phylogenetic signal, meaning the K value is rather truthfully small here.  I think we were pretty clear in the paper that one should call it phylogenetic signal when both the effect size is large and lambda suggests the data look like they were sampled from a BM process.  The latter thing is not at all true and former thing is subjectively also not true, even if the P-value is borderline true.

Generally if P = 0.05 one would expect Z = 1.96, so you might also have an issue with strangely distributed residuals in your GLS fits.

I think that covers most bases — hope it made sense.

Best,
Mike

What the burn-in method does is use a smaller number of permutations (I think about 10% of the total requested) to find Z scores in intervals, and then fits a spline to find where Z — not lambda! — is maximized.  Once found, then the full set of permutations is run for a lambda value that corresponds to the preliminary Z maximization, obtaining a Z from that full distribution.
>
> There are two ways the burn-in method of optimization can go haywire.  One is if there is a flat surface for which to fit a spline.  In these cases, Z would probably be small, wherever it is optimized, and whether it was optimized appropriately, since finding a maximum in a surface that is flat is fraught with potential error.  Second is if one is trying to optimize a multivariate lambda (assuming two or more variables) with a single variable, in which case the burn-in method makes no sense.  This is like asking the analysis to ignore the larger number of requested permutations for a straightforward analysis and have it make a biased judgement first based on a distribution with 10% of the permutations.  (A good future argument will be to have the number of burn-in permutations as an option, but as stated in the help file, optimization strategies are still in need of development.)
>
> In practical terms, you should XX-out all burn-in results in your table except for shape.  It is illogical to perform that optimization, a lesson we will have to fix on the next software version to prevent a silly trial.
>
> Finally, regarding your Avg. Body Weight result, it is good to remember what is happening in the analysis, because although statistical results like this seem odd, they can make sense.  The lambda is practically 0.  The significant P-value indicates that lambda = 0.0000007 — basically a star phylogeny with the tiniest bit of structure near the root of the tree, so small as to be easily ignored — has a result to suggest the trace of the generalized least squares residual variance you find with the covariance matrix used from this result is smaller than expected by chance.  You *could* call that phylogenetic signal but you would be foolish to suggest it resembles what you would expect with Brownian Motion, which tends to be what we use as a standard to think about phylogenetic signal, meaning the K value is rather truthfully small here.  I think we were pretty clear in the paper that one should call it phylogenetic signal when both the effect size is large and lambda suggests the data look like they were sampled from a BM process.  The latter thing is not at all true and former thing is subjectively also not true, even if the P-value is borderline true.
>

I have a question about the phenotypic trajectory analysis and standard PCA.

I first performed a PCA on all the specimens (living taxa and fossils) in the sample (Analysis1).
The lving sample consists of 3 age groups (juveniles, adolenscents and adults) across three taxa, and fossils are two juvenile and three adult specimens.

I read a paper by Mori and Harvati (2019) <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ajpa.23926>, they said "we added the fossil samples to the PCA calculated on the convriance matrix of our extant samples by projecting each individual on the original PC axes." I am kind of confused whether I did the same thing or not.

In this case, can I know why the two pca plots are different and what should I do to project the fossils? Thanks very much for your help!

Best regards,
Xue

Xue,

If you used the trajectory.analysis function, PCA is performed on the trajectories points (fitted values), not the entire data set (should be clear by the axis labels).  The entire data are projected on these axes, and trajectory points can be added, providing the best picture of trajectory variation rather than variation in the data.  You can extract the LS means from the analysis, if you prefer, and project those onto standard PCs.

Projection is simply (1) mean-centering your data and (2) multiplying them times the rotation matrix you get from either PCA.  You can project your data, other data with the same variables, other estimates, or some other logical points onto the axes.  The two PCAs are different rotations of the same data space, regardless which you prefer to use.

Best,
Mike
